content_html:
100 words - Linguistic theories

The sorting is a frame‑guided, metaphor‑licensed, prototype‑ordered itinerary. We first cluster by semantic field (lexical semantics), sequence clusters according to a Seeing → Attending → Remembering → Organising → Accessing → Evaluating → Reflecting script (frame semantics & scripts), advance from concrete to abstract via SEEING → KNOWING metaphors (conceptual metaphor), and preserve local coherence (discourse theories). The endgame (insight, wisdom, understanding) reflects blending and higher‑order construal.

Overview

The ordering groups words into a path from concrete perceptual phenomena (optics, appearance) through attentional and mnemonic mechanisms (encoding, storage, retrieval), then to metacognitive control and finally to insight and understanding. The design draws on mainstream approaches in lexical semantics, cognitive linguistics, and discourse/pragmatics.

Lexical semantics: fields, relations, prototypes

  • Semantic fields & lexical sets. Terms cluster by domain (e.g., optics vs. memory), enabling phase-based grouping (Cruse; Murphy).
  • Lexical relations. Synonymy/antonymy, hyponymy/hypernymy, and meronymy keep near-neighbors together (e.g., clarity ↔ opacity).
  • Prototype theory & radial categories. Within a phase, ordering often goes from prototypical items (mirror) to peripheral artifacts (bloom) (Rosch; Lakoff).

Frame semantics & scripts

  • Frame semantics (Fillmore). Words evoke structured situations (frames). The phases align with frames like Seeing → Attending → Remembering → Retrieving → Evaluating.
  • Scripts/schemas (Schank & Abelson; Bartlett). The macro-order reflects a culturally familiar event-sequence: perceive → attend → encode → store → organize → retrieve → evaluate → reflect.

Conceptual metaphor & image schemas

  • Conceptual metaphor (Lakoff & Johnson). Mappings like SEEING IS KNOWING, KNOWLEDGE IS CLARITY, and UNDERSTANDING IS VISION justify transitions from optical clarity to cognitive clarity.
  • Image schemas (Johnson; Lakoff). The path follows SOURCE–PATH–GOAL: from stimulus (source), through handling (path), to understanding (goal).
  • Force dynamics (Talmy). Items like attention, filtering reflect dynamic control over input, structuring the path.

Cognitive grammar & conceptual integration

  • Cognitive grammar (Langacker). Meaning as conceptualization motivates moving from grounded perception to increasingly abstract construal.
  • Conceptual blending (Fauconnier & Turner). Later phases (imagination, insight) blend memory structures with current context to yield novel structure on the way to understanding.

Distributional & usage-based semantics

  • Distributional hypothesis (Harris) & vector semantics. Words that occur in similar contexts cluster (e.g., encoding–storage–retrieval), supporting the grouping dimension.
  • Usage-based models (Goldberg; Bybee). Frequency and constructions shape salience and typical sequencing of operations.

Pragmatics & discourse coherence

  • Rhetorical Structure Theory (Mann & Thompson). The whole sequence functions like a discourse with nucleus–satellite relations (preparation → result), justifying a left-to-right build-up.
  • Centering & coherence (Grosz et al.). Local neighborhoods keep topical coherence (optics-group, memory-group) before topic shifts.
  • Gricean relevance. The order prefers informationally progressive steps (from observable surface to abstract conclusion).

Psycholinguistic alignment (supporting, not prescriptive)

  • Levels of processing & working memory (Craik–Lockhart; Baddeley–Hitch). Attention → encoding → consolidation → retrieval mirrors widely taught memory architecture, lending cognitive plausibility to the lexical path.
  • Encoding specificity (Tulving & Thomson). The “organization → access” phases reflect how structure aids retrieval.
